181: Hill addresses the belief that material success results from favorable breaks. While there's some truth, those depending entirely on luck are nearly always disappointed because they overlook the knowledge needed to make favorable breaks to order. He shares examples: W. C. Fields, the comedian, lost all his money during the Depression, found vaudeville obsolete, was past 60, and fell injuring his neck—yet he was PERSISTENT, offered to work without pay in movies, and eventually got his breaks. Marie Dressler was down and out at about 60 with money gone and no job, but her PERSISTENCE brought an astounding triumph late in life. Eddie Cantor lost his money in the 1929 crash but still had PERSISTENCE and courage, exploiting himself back into $10,000 a week. The only break anyone can afford to rely upon is a self-made one, through application of PERSISTENCE, starting with DEFINITENESS OF PURPOSE. Hill challenges readers to examine the first 100 people they meet, ask what they want most—98 cannot tell. Some say SECURITY, MONEY, HAPPINESS, FAME, POWER, or SOCIAL RECOGNITION, but none can define these terms or give a PLAN. Riches do not respond to wishes.
182: Hill states riches respond only to definite plans, backed by definite desires, through constant PERSISTENCE. Under 'How To Develop Persistence,' he presents four simple steps requiring no great intelligence, education, or time: (1) A DEFINITE PURPOSE BACKED BY BURNING DESIRE FOR ITS FULFILLMENT. (2) A DEFINITE PLAN, EXPRESSED IN CONTINUOUS ACTION. (3) A MIND CLOSED TIGHTLY AGAINST ALL NEGATIVE AND DISCOURAGING INFLUENCES, including negative suggestions of relatives, friends, and acquaintances. (4) A FRIENDLY ALLIANCE WITH ONE OR MORE PERSONS WHO WILL ENCOURAGE ONE TO FOLLOW THROUGH WITH BOTH PLAN AND PURPOSE. These four steps are essential for success in all walks of life. The entire purpose of the 13 principles is to enable one to take these steps as habit. They control economic destiny, lead to freedom and independence of thought, lead to riches, power, fame, and worldly recognition. They guarantee favorable breaks, convert dreams into physical realities, and lead to mastery of FEAR, DISCOURAGEMENT, and INDIFFERENCE. The magnificent reward is the privilege of writing one's own ticket and making life yield whatever price is asked. Hill then introduces Mrs. Wallis Simpson's story as an example of persistence, suggesting her great love was not accidental but resulted from burning desire and careful searching at every step.
183: Hill discusses Wallis Simpson's persistence: her first duty was to love. Jesus called love the greatest thing on earth—not manmade rules, criticism, bitterness, or slander, but love. Simpson knew what she wanted long before meeting the Prince of Wales. Twice when she failed to find it, she had courage to continue searching. 'To thine own self be true, and it must follow, as the night the day, thou canst not then be false to any man.' Her rise from obscurity was slow, progressive, PERSISTENT, but SURE. She triumphed over unbelievably long odds—an astounding example of applied PERSISTENCE and self-determination. Hill then asks what lesson may be learned from King Edward's part in this drama. The king came into the world without his own consent, born to great riches he didn't request, persistently sought in marriage by politicians tossing princesses at his feet. He inherited a crown he didn't seek. For over 40 years he was not a free agent, had little privacy, and assumed duties inflicted upon him. Despite all privileges of crown, money, fame, and power, there was an emptiness fillable only by love. His greatest DESIRE was for love, felt long before meeting Wallis Simpson, tugging at his heart and crying for expression.
184: Hill reflects on King Edward's DECISION to give up the British crown for the woman he loved—a decision requiring courage and having a price. As a suggestion to anyone finding fault with the Duke of Windsor, Hill notes his 'open declaration' wasn't essential—he could have followed the custom of clandestine liaison prevailing in Europe for centuries without giving up his throne or the woman. But this unusual man was built of sterner stuff; his love was deep and sincere, representing the one thing above ALL ELSE he truly DESIRED, so he took what he wanted and paid the price demanded. Most of the world would applaud the Duke and Wallis Simpson for their PERSISTENCE in searching until they found life's greatest reward. ALL CAN PROFIT by following their example. Hill then asks what mystical power gives persistent people the capacity to master difficulties—whether persistence sets up spiritual, mental, or chemical activity giving access to supernatural forces, whether Infinite Intelligence throws itself on the side of those who fight on after the battle is lost. He cites Henry Ford, who started from scratch with little but PERSISTENCE, and Thomas Edison, who with less than three months of schooling became the world's leading inventor. From firsthand study of both over many years, Hill found no quality save PERSISTENCE that even remotely suggested the major source of their stupendous achievements.
185: Hill states that an impartial study of prophets, philosophers, miracle workers, and religious leaders leads to the inevitable conclusion that PERSISTENCE, concentration of effort, and DEFINITENESS OF PURPOSE were the major sources of their achievements. He presents the story of Mohammed as an example. Mohammed was a prophet who never performed a miracle, had no formal schooling, and didn't begin his mission until 40. When he announced he was God's Messenger, he was ridiculed and labeled a lunatic. He was banished from Mecca, his followers stripped of worldly goods and sent into the desert. After 10 years of preaching, he had nothing but banishment, poverty, and ridicule. Yet before another 10 years passed, he was ruler of Mecca and head of a new world religion that swept to the Danube and Pyrenees. His impetus was threefold: the power of words, the efficacy of prayer, and man's kinship with God. Mohammed was born to impoverished members of a leading Mecca family. Because Mecca was unsanitary, children were sent to be raised in the desert by Bedouins. Mohammed tended sheep and hired out to a rich widow as caravan leader, traveling the Eastern World, observing Christianity's decline into warring sects. At 28, the widow Khadija married him. For 12 years he was a respected, shrewd trader. Then he took to wandering the desert and returned with the first verse of the Koran, saying the archangel Gabriel had appeared and declared him Messenger of God.
186: Hill continues Mohammed's story: the Koran, the revealed word of God, was the closest thing to a miracle in Mohammed's life. He had not been a poet with no gift of words, yet the Koran's verses were better than any professional poets could produce—to the Arabs, this was a miracle, as the gift of words was the greatest gift. The Koran declared all men equal before God and the world should be a democratic state—Islam. This political heresy, plus Mohammed's desire to destroy the 360 idols in the Caaba courtyard, brought his banishment. The idols brought desert tribes to Mecca for trade, so the businessmen (capitalists, of which Mohammed had been one) set upon him. He retreated to the desert and demanded sovereignty over the world. The rise of Islam began—out of the desert came a flame that would not be extinguished: a democratic army fighting as a unit, prepared to die without wincing. Mohammed invited Jews and Christians to join him, not building a new religion but calling all who believed in one God to a single faith. If they had accepted, Islam would have conquered the world. They didn't, and wouldn't even accept Mohammed's innovation of humane warfare. When his armies entered Jerusalem, not a single person was killed for faith. When crusaders entered centuries later, not a Moslem was spared. But Christians did accept one Moslem idea—the university.
187: Hill concludes that religious visionaries like Mohammed, business leaders like Edison, Ford, and Carnegie, political leaders like Samuel Adams, entertainers like Fannie Hurst, Kate Smith, and W. C. Fields, and cosmopolites like Wallis Simpson and the Duke of Windsor—all demonstrate the tremendous power of The Eighth Step to Riches: PERSISTENCE, sustained effort in the face of all odds and adversity. PERSISTENCE creates FAITH. FAITH is the only known antidote for failure, the starting point of all accumulation of riches, and the only agency through which one can tap the force of Infinite Intelligence. The page concludes with the statement: 'GREAT POWER CAN BE ACCUMULATED THROUGH NO OTHER PRINCIPLE THAN THAT OF THE MASTER MIND!'—transitioning to Chapter 9.
188: This page opens Chapter 9: POWER OF THE MASTER MIND—The Driving Force (The Ninth Step to Riches). Hill states: PERSISTENCE creates FAITH, from FAITH comes POWER, and POWER is essential for success in accumulating money. PLANS alone are inert without sufficient POWER to translate them into ACTION. POWER is defined as 'organized and intelligently directed KNOWLEDGE'—ORGANIZED effort sufficient to transmute DESIRE into its monetary equivalent, produced through coordination of two or more people working toward a DEFINITE end in a spirit of harmony. POWER IS REQUIRED FOR THE ACCUMULATION OF MONEY and for its RETENTION. He identifies 'The Three Major Sources of Knowledge': (1) INFINITE INTELLIGENCE—contacted with the aid of Creative Imagination. (2) ACCUMULATED EXPERIENCE—found in public libraries, taught in schools and colleges. (3) EXPERIMENT AND RESEARCH—gathering, classifying, and organizing new facts daily in science and other fields, often requiring Creative Imagination.
189: Hill explains that knowledge from these sources may be converted into POWER by organizing it into definite PLANS expressed in terms of ACTION. If plans are comprehensive, one must generally induce others to cooperate before injecting the necessary element of POWER. Under 'Gaining Power through the Master Mind,' he defines the Master Mind as: 'Coordination of knowledge and effort, in a spirit of harmony between two or more people, for the attainment of a definite purpose.' No individual can have great power without availing themselves of the Master Mind Principle. If one carries out Chapter 1's instructions with PERSISTENCE and intelligence, selecting the Master Mind Group with discrimination, the objective will be halfway reached even before recognizing it. He explains the two characteristics of the Master Mind Principle: one economic, one psychic. The economic feature is obvious—economic advantages are created by surrounding oneself with advice, counsel, and cooperation of people willing to lend wholehearted aid in PERFECT HARMONY. This cooperative alliance has been the basis of nearly every great fortune. The psychic phase is more abstract, referring to spiritual forces. The key statement: 'No two minds ever come together without, thereby, creating a third, invisible, intangible force which may be likened to a third mind.'
190: Hill elaborates on the psychic phase of the Master Mind. There are only two known substances—energy and matter. Matter can be broken into molecules, atoms, protons, neutrons, and electrons. Likewise, there are units of energy. The human mind is a form of energy, partly spiritual. When two minds coordinate in a SPIRIT OF HARMONY, the spiritual units of energy form an 'affinity' constituting the psychic phase of the Master Mind. The economic feature was first called to Hill's attention by Andrew Carnegie during his earliest research years—discovery of this principle was responsible for Hill's choice of life's work. Carnegie's Master Mind Group consisted of approximately 50 individuals with whom he surrounded himself for manufacturing and marketing steel. He attributed his entire fortune to the POWER accumulated through this Master Mind. Analyze anyone who has accumulated a great or modest fortune, and you will find they either consciously or unconsciously employed the Master Mind Principle. GREAT POWER CAN BE ACCUMULATED THROUGH NO OTHER PRINCIPLE!
